source_text: Timiditatis est autem, cum te alius per deos suos obligat iuratione uel aliqua testificatione et tu, ne intellegaris, quiescis. nam aeque quiescendo confirmas maiestatem eorum, cuius causa uideberis obligatus. quid refert, deos nationum dicendo deos an audiendo confirmes? iures per idola, an ab alio adiuratus acquiescas? cur non agnoscamus uersutias satanae, qui, quod ore nostro perficere non potest, id agit, ut suorum ore per- Sciat per aures inferens nobis idololatriam? certe quisquis ille est, aut amica aut inimica congressione adstringit. si inimica, iam ad pugnam uocaris et scis tibi dimicandum esse: si amica, quanto securius in dominum transferes sponsionem tuam, ut dissoluas obligationem eius, per quem te malus honori idolorum id est idololatriae quaerebat annectere. omnis patientia eiusmodi idololatria. honoras eos, quibus impositis obsequium praestitisti. scio quendam, cui dominus ignoscat, cum illi in publico per litem dictum esset: Iupiter tibi sit iratus, respondisse: immo tibi. quid aliter fecisset ethnicus, qui Iouem deum credidit? etiamsi non per eundem retorsisset maledictum nec per ullum Iouis similem, confirmauerat Iouem deum, per quem se maledictum indigne tulisse demonstrauerat remaledicens. ad quid enim indigneris per eum, quem scis nihil esse? nam si insanis, iam esse confirmas, et erit idololatria professio timoris tui: quanto magis, cum per ipsum remaledicis, eodem Iouis honorem facis, quo et ille, qui te prouocauit? fidelis autem in eiusmodi ridere debet, non insanire, immo, secundum praeceptum, ne per deum quidem remaledicere, sed plane benedicere per deum, ut et idola destruas et deum praedices et adimpleas disciplinam.
orientation: Tertullian is warning that even passive acceptance of pagan oaths or curses honors idols, and he is about to give examples of how a Christian should respond.
pass_a_gloss: But it is of timidity, when another binds you by an oath through his gods or by some testimony and you, so that you may not be understood, keep quiet. For equally by keeping quiet you confirm their majesty, by whose cause you will seem to have been bound. What does it matter, whether by saying the gods of the nations as gods or by hearing you confirm them? Whether you swear by idols, or being adjured by another you acquiesce? Why should we not recognize the cunning of Satan, who, what he cannot accomplish through our mouth, this he works, so that through the mouth of his own he may bring idolatry into us through the ears? Certainly whoever he is, he binds either by friendly or by hostile encounter. If hostile, already you are called to battle and you know that you must fight: if friendly, how much more safely will you transfer your pledge to the Lord, so that you may dissolve the obligation of him, through whom the evil one was seeking to attach you to the honor of idols, that is to idolatry. All patience of this kind is idolatry. You honor those, to whom, when they were imposed, you have shown compliance. I know a certain man, may the Lord pardon him, when it was said to him in public through a quarrel: May Jupiter be angry with you, he answered: rather with you. What else would a pagan have done, who believed Jupiter to be a god? Even if he had not hurled back the curse through the same god nor through any similar to Jupiter, he had confirmed Jupiter as a god, through whom he had shown that he had borne the curse undeservedly by cursing back. For why would you be indignant through him, whom you know to be nothing? For if you rage, already you confirm that he exists, and the profession of your fear will be idolatry: how much more, when you curse back through him, do you do the same honor to Jupiter, as also he who provoked you? But a believer in such a case ought to laugh, not to rage, indeed, according to the precept, not even to curse back through God, but plainly to bless through God, so that you may both destroy idols and proclaim God and fulfill the discipline.

choices.why: Fixed glossary term; must use 'idolatry' not 'idol worship'.
Literal rendering of the phrase; 'nations' is the standard term for pagans in Tertullian, and the glossary bans 'Gentiles' for ethnici but this phrase is literal.

choices.english: bringing idolatry into us through the ears
choices.why: Literal sense of the metaphor; keeps the physical image of idolatry entering through hearing.
rejected: instilling idolatry in us by hearing

choices.why: Literal rendering of sponsio as a pledge or promise; keeps the legal/contractual sense.
Fixed glossary term; must use 'discipline' for disciplina.

pass_b_english: It is timidity when someone else binds you by an oath or some testimony sworn by his gods, and you keep quiet so as not to be found out. For by keeping quiet you equally confirm their majesty, since you will seem to be bound for their sake. What difference does it make whether you confirm the gods of the nations by naming them as gods or by hearing them named? Whether you swear by idols, or, when adjured by another, you acquiesce?

Why do we not recognize the cunning of Satan? When he cannot accomplish it through our own mouth, he works to bring idolatry into us through the ears by the mouth of his own people. Certainly, whoever he is, he binds you either in a friendly or a hostile encounter. If hostile, you are already called to battle, and you know you must fight. If friendly, how much more safely will you transfer your oath to the Lord, so that you may dissolve the obligation of the one through whom the evil one was seeking to attach you to the honor of idols, that is, to idolatry.

All patience of this kind is idolatry. You honor those to whom you have shown compliance when they imposed themselves on you. I know a man—may the Lord pardon him—who, when it was said to him publicly in a dispute, 'May Jupiter be angry with you,' answered, 'No, with you.' What else would a pagan have done, who believed Jupiter to be a god? Even if he had not hurled back the curse by the same god, nor by any god like Jupiter, he had confirmed Jupiter as a god, since by cursing back he showed that he had borne the curse undeservedly through him. For why would you be angry through one whom you know to be nothing? If you rage, you already confirm that he exists, and the profession of your fear will be idolatry. How much more, when you curse back by him, do you do the same honor to Jupiter as the one who provoked you?

But a believer in such cases ought to laugh, not rage—indeed, according to the command, not even to curse back by a god, but plainly to bless by God, so that you both destroy idols and proclaim God and fulfill the discipline.
notes: The source text contains a line break and possible corruption: 'per- Sciat per aures' appears to be a damaged passage. The gloss renders the sense as 'through the mouth of his own he may bring idolatry into us through the ears,' treating 'per-' as the start of 'per aures' and 'Sciat' as possibly a corruption or misplaced word. No text has been invented; the gloss follows the visible words as closely as possible.

last_rejected.quote: If you rage, you already confirm that he exists, and the profession of your fear will be idolatry.
last_rejected.source_quote: nam si insanis, iam esse confirmas, et erit idololatria professio timoris tui
last_rejected.why: "insanis" means "if you act foolishly/insane", not "if you rage"; the English changes the sense.
last_rejected.fix: If you act foolishly, you already confirm his existence, and the profession of your fear will be idolatry.
last_rejected.ruling: insanis ranges from 'be mad/insane' to 'rage'; 'rage' fits cursing-back context and is acceptable within word's range.

problems.quote: May Jupiter be angry with you
since by cursing back he showed that he had been unworthily cursed by one through whom he was angry
problems.why: Circular and convoluted; 'through whom he was angry' is opaque.
problems.fix: Simplify to 'since by cursing back he acknowledged Jupiter's power'.

problems.quote: transfer your pledge to the Lord
problems.why: 'Transfer pledge' is unclear; likely 'redirect your oath to the Lord'.
problems.fix: Change to 'redirect your oath to the Lord'.

problems.quote: not even to curse back by a god, but plainly to bless by God
problems.why: Romans 12:14 says 'bless and do not curse'; 'by God' is addition.
problems.fix: Note Tertullian's expansion of Pauline command.

fixed: Speaker problem: the source does not identify the speaker of the curse; the English already presents it as reported speech within the anecdote, so no edit is needed.

Unreadable: the source says 'per quem se maledictum indigne tulisse demonstrauerat remaledicens' — he showed he had borne the curse undeservedly through him by cursing back. The English was convoluted; simplified while keeping the source meaning.
Mistranslation: 'sponsionem' means pledge/oath; 'oath' is clearer than 'pledge' here, so changed.

Wrong scripture: the source says 'ne per deum quidem remaledicere, sed plane benedicere per deum' — not even to curse back through God, but plainly to bless through God. The English matches the source; no edit needed.

polish.changed: Clarified the objector's curse as a quoted speech, smoothed the convoluted sentence about cursing back by Jupiter, clarified 'transfer your oath to the Lord' as redirecting the oath, and kept the final blessing command as Tertullian states it without adding a Scripture reference.
